chunks: RISC-V: ISA or microarchitecture. The question: Does RISC-V specify the ISA or microarchitecture?
RISC-V is an ISA, which means it is a specification. It defines the instructions, registers and rules that software can see.
It does not say how many pipeline stages a chip has, whether it runs instructions out of order, or how big its caches are.
Those choices are the microarchitecture, and each RISC-V chip makes its own.
Think of a piece of sheet music. The score fixes which notes are played and in what order. A school band and a full orchestra can both play it.
They differ in speed, size and cost. RISC-V is the score, and each chip design is a different orchestra. The score does set some rules every performer must respect.
Everything above the Microarchitecture box constrains behavior software can see. Everything below is the implementer's freedom.
Profiles exist to stop the top of the stack from fragmenting into incompatible extension combinations.
ISA: the contract between software and hardware ("What is an ISA?") Microarchitecture: a chip's internal design that carries out the ISA ("What is microarchitecture?")
Core: one specific processor design that implements the ISA. Pipeline, out-of-order, cache: internal speed tricks.
They overlap the steps of several instructions, run instructions as soon as their inputs are ready, and keep recent data in a small fast memory.
Extension: an optional standard addition to the ISA. Software only runs on cores that have the extensions it needs.
Take one loop of 8 instructions per pass, with one hard-to-predict branch and one load that sometimes misses the cache.
Run the identical RISC-V binary (compiled program) on three cores. The page's illustrative model gives 8. 8 cycles per pass on simple core A, 8. 9 on core B, and 4.
5 on a wide out-of-order core C. At 1 gigahertz for A and B, and 2 gigahertz for C, the times are 8. 8 nanoseconds, 8. 9 nanoseconds and 2. 25 nanoseconds.
That is roughly a 4 times gap with the same software. That is the whole idea: "RISC-V" says nothing about speed.
"It specifies the ISA. RISC-V defines the instructions, registers, privilege modes, traps, virtual memory and memory model, but not the pipeline, caches or branch predictor.
Those are microarchitecture, chosen by whoever builds the core.
That's why in-order cores like Rocket and out-of-order cores like BOOM can both be RISC-V and run the same software at very different speeds and power."
